answer:
Simulate the classical de Vahl Davis natural convection benchmark in a 2D square cavity of side L = 1 m using OpenFOAM.
Use the solver buoyantBoussinesqPimpleFoam (not laplacianFoam).
The cavity is filled with air treated with the Boussinesq approximation.
Operate at Rayleigh number Ra = 10³ with Prandtl number Pr ≈ 0.71 and thermal expansion coefficient β ≈ 1/295 K⁻¹.
With ΔT = 10 K and L = 1 m, set the kinematic viscosity ν (together with the diffusivity α = ν/Pr) so that Ra = g β ΔT L³ / (ν α) = 10³ is achieved; the exact values must be computed consistently from this relation.
Use gravitational acceleration g = (0 -9.81 0).
Use reference temperature T_ref = 295 K for the Boussinesq term.
The left wall is hot with fixedValue T = 300 K.
The right wall is cold with fixedValue T = 290 K.
The top and bottom walls are adiabatic with zeroGradient temperature (the earlier suggestion of fixedValue T = 295 K was retracted by the user).
All four walls use noSlip for velocity.
Treat the flow as laminar with no turbulence model (simulationType laminar in turbulenceProperties).
Create a uniform mesh of 100×100 cells in x and y with 1 cell in z, using empty boundary conditions on the front and back patches for the 2D case.
Initialize the fields at rest (U = 0) with a uniform temperature T = 295 K.
Run the simulation until steady state, monitoring the average Nusselt number on the hot (left) wall and considering steady state reached when its relative variation between monitoring intervals falls below approximately 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵.
Set a generous fixed end time (e.g. t = 1000 s or more) as a safeguard stop criterion.
Compute the average Nusselt number on the hot wall and compare it against the de Vahl Davis reference value Nu ≈ 1.117–1.118 for Ra = 10³.
Additionally save the velocity and temperature fields to visualize the convection cell.
Also report the maximum horizontal velocity along the vertical centerline and the maximum vertical velocity along the horizontal centerline, as these are standard benchmark metrics.
